newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH REFINERY GROUP SEEKS STRATEGIC INVESTOR.
newsitem.headline: POLISH REFINERY GROUP SEEKS STRATEGIC INVESTOR.

text.p: A group of Polish firms, which wants to build a $2.3 billion refinery, is seeking a strategic investor who would take more than 51 percent of shares in the venture, a group official said.

Konstanty Chmielewski, head of the group's executive office, told reporters on Monday foreign investors from the chemical and financial sectors were interested in participating but were waiting for the treasury to declare the extent of its potential involvement in the scheme.
"Shareholders have decided to open the venture to a strategic investor, who could take more than 51 percent," said Chmielewski.

"Foreign chemical firms and investment funds are interested in taking a controlling stake above 51 percent in the future company, but they wait for the treasury to declare the extent of its potential involvement," he said.

The new refinery in the southern town of Kedzierzyn-Kozle would process six million tons of crude oil annually and fill the fuel deficit on the Polish market, estimated at 2.3 million tons this year. Construction work would last three years.
The consortium includes the Kedzierzyn nitrogen works, the Ciech chemicals trader, the CPN fuel distributor, Bank Slaski, Kredyt Bank , Rafako , Remak, Mostostal Zabrze and PBR .
The group wants the government to declare if it would grant the refinery tax breaks, create a special economic zone there, buy 10 to 15 percent of the company's stock or extend credit guarantees.
"We would like to the government to make up its mind so that we can set up a company to start the construction by the end of the first half of 1997 at the latest," Chmielewski said.
He added however, that if the government decided not to participate in the venture, the time of return on the investment would lengthen to seven years from five years.
In October the government's economic committee (KERM) decided the construction of the refinery would not be a government programme, but it is due to discuss the venture again later in November.
Poland now has seven state-owned refineries, which supply more then 80 percent of the country's fuel needs.
